Runtime Validation Mental Model
Why TypeScript types are not runtime validation and where trust boundaries belong

Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
JSON crosses the network

↓

Schema validates at runtime

↓

Service applies business rules

↓

Database enforces persistence constraints

Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic.

Static types are not a firewall
A TypeScript annotation exists for the compiler and editor. By the time JSON arrives over HTTP, the sender is
not constrained by your TypeScript source code. Postman, PowerShell, a browser, a mobile app, or a malicious
caller can send any syntactically valid JSON value.

type CreateTaskInput = {
projectId: string;
title: string;
};

// This type cannot stop a network caller from sending:
{
"projectId": 123,
"title": false,
"admin": true
}

Figure 1 - Trust boundary
External caller

↓

HTTP / JSON

↓

Runtime validation boundary

↓

Controller receives validated value

↓

Service applies business rules

↓

Prisma persists valid domain data

Validation belongs at the system boundary because that is where untrusted external data enters trusted application code.

Validation vs business rules vs database constraints
Question                               Best first owner                         Example

Is this input shaped correctly?        Validation schema                        title is a non-empty string

Is this request allowed by the         Service/business logic                   assignee belongs to workspace
domain?

Must this invariant hold for           Database constraint                      foreign key references a real Project
persisted rows?

Strong systems usually use all three layers. Validation is not a replacement for database constraints, and
database constraints are not a replacement for meaningful application rules.

DTO does not have to mean class
In older NestJS examples, DTO usually means a class decorated with class-validator annotations. NestJS 12
adds a first-class schema-first workflow. In this course, a DTO means the validated data shape crossing the
HTTP boundary. We infer the TypeScript DTO type from the Zod schema instead of manually duplicating it in a
class.

export const createTaskSchema = z.strictObject({
projectId: z.uuid(),
title: z.string().trim().min(1).max(200),
});

export type CreateTaskDto =
z.infer<typeof createTaskSchema>;

One source of truth

The schema is executable at runtime and also produces the TypeScript type. This removes a common source of drift
where validation says one thing while a separately maintained interface says another.

Parsing may also transform
Validation libraries can do more than return yes/no. Trimming, coercion, defaults, and transformations can
change the value that crosses the boundary. For that reason, think in terms of input -> parse -> validated
output rather than input -> boolean.

Figure 2 - Parse lifecycle
raw JSON value

↓

Zod schema

↓

validated / transformed output

↓

controller parameter

The controller should operate on the parsed output, not on the raw body.

Zod 4 + NestJS 12 Standard Schema
Install Zod, lock the version, and use NestJS 12 built-in schema-first validation

Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
Zod schema metadata

↓

StandardSchemaValidationPipe

↓

validated controller parameter

Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic.

STEP 1 - Install Zod in the API package
Zod belongs to apps/api because Phase 12 uses it to validate NestJS request inputs. Do not add it to the
monorepo root merely because multiple applications might use it someday.

From taskflow\apps\api run:

pnpm add zod@4.6.5

Then verify the package version from the same directory:

pnpm list zod

Course lock

Zod 4.6.5 is locked for this phase. If a newer patch appears later, keep the book series internally consistent unless
the course is intentionally upgraded.

Why Zod in this course?
• Schema definitions execute at runtime.

• The same schema can infer TypeScript types.

• Zod implements the Standard Schema interface used by NestJS 12.

• It works in Node.js and browsers, which gives us future reuse options without forcing shared packages today.

• The API can express strict object boundaries, enums, UUIDs, string rules, nullable fields, and custom
refinements.

NestJS 12 changed the recommended teaching path
Historically, many NestJS courses used class-validator + class-transformer or a custom ZodValidationPipe.
Those approaches still exist. NestJS 12, however, added first-class Standard Schema support to route
parameter decorators and a built-in StandardSchemaValidationPipe.

Approach                                        Good fit                                 TaskFlow Phase 12

ValidationPipe + class-validator                Existing class-decorator DTO projects    Not selected

Custom Zod pipe                                 Older Nest versions / special behavior   Not necessary

StandardSchemaValidationPipe + Zod              Schema-first NestJS 12 projects          Selected

STEP 2 - Register validation globally
The route decorators will attach schema metadata. The global pipe is what actually validates that metadata
before the controller handler runs.

import { StandardSchemaValidationPipe } from "@nestjs/common";

// inside bootstrap()
app.useGlobalPipes(new StandardSchemaValidationPipe());

Figure 1 - NestJS validation position

Fastify receives request

↓

Nest resolves route parameters

↓

StandardSchemaValidationPipe validates schema metadata

↓

Controller method is invoked

↓

Service runs

When schema validation fails, the controller method is not called.

Do not validate twice

Once the schema is attached to @Body() or @Param() and the global StandardSchemaValidationPipe is registered,
do not immediately call createTaskSchema.parse(body) again inside the service. That would duplicate the boundary
work.

Task Schemas & Inferred DTOs
Create/update schemas, UUIDs, enums, nullable fields, strict objects, and DTO
inference

Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
field schemas

↓

request object schemas

↓

z.infer DTO types

Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic.

Create the Task schemas
Replace the temporary tasks.types.ts idea from Phase 11 with a schema-first file. The schema is now the
boundary contract; DTO types are inferred from it.

import { z } from "zod";
import {
TaskPriority,
TaskStatus,
} from "../generated/prisma/client";

const taskTitleSchema = z
.string()
.trim()
.min(1)
.max(200);

const taskDescriptionSchema = z
.string()
.trim()
.max(2000)
.nullable();

export const taskIdSchema = z.uuid();

export const createTaskSchema = z.strictObject({
projectId: z.uuid(),
title: taskTitleSchema,
description: taskDescriptionSchema.optional(),
});

export const updateTaskSchema = z
.strictObject({
title: taskTitleSchema.optional(),
description: taskDescriptionSchema.optional(),
status: z.enum(TaskStatus).optional(),
priority: z.enum(TaskPriority).optional(),
})
.refine(
(value) => Object.keys(value).length > 0,
"At least one updatable field must be provided.",
);

export type CreateTaskDto = z.infer<typeof createTaskSchema>;
export type UpdateTaskDto = z.infer<typeof updateTaskSchema>;

Why z.strictObject?
A normal object schema can choose how to handle unknown keys. For API request bodies in this phase, we
deliberately reject unknown properties. This catches misspellings and prevents clients from assuming
unsupported fields are accepted.

{
"projectId": "...",
"title": "Ship feature",
"admin": true
}

// strict object => reject "admin"

Reject vs strip

Silently stripping unknown fields can be useful in some systems. TaskFlow chooses rejection at the API boundary
because a 400 response exposes client mistakes early and makes the request contract explicit.

Title rules
• string: callers cannot submit numbers, booleans, arrays, or objects as a title.

• trim: whitespace at both ends is normalized before the service receives it.

• min(1): a string containing only spaces becomes empty after trim and fails.

• max(200): request payload size and domain expectations are bounded.

Nullable and optional are different
Shape                                           Meaning

description omitted                             Client did not provide this field

description: null                               Client explicitly clears / sets no description

description: "text"                             Client supplies a description

This distinction becomes especially useful for PATCH semantics, where omitted means “do not change” while
null can mean “clear the current value.”

Enums come from the generated domain model
TaskStatus and TaskPriority are imported from the generated Prisma client so the validation vocabulary
remains aligned with the domain enum vocabulary already used by persistence.

Update schema: all fields optional, empty object forbidden
PATCH should permit any supported subset of fields, but an empty update does not express a meaningful
change. The refine rule makes that contract explicit.

.refine(
(value) => Object.keys(value).length > 0,
"At least one updatable field must be provided.",
);

Create Task Validation
Validate POST bodies before Project lookup or Prisma persistence

Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
POST /tasks

↓

createTaskSchema

↓

service Project check

↓

Prisma create

Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic.

POST /tasks - validate before creating
The create endpoint is an ideal place to see the validation boundary because it accepts multiple fields and then
performs a real parent-existence business check.

Figure 1 - Valid create request
POST JSON

↓

createTaskSchema parses

↓

TasksController.create

↓

TasksService verifies Project

↓

Prisma INSERT

↓

201 Created

Input validation is first; business validation and persistence follow.

Valid request
{
"projectId": "3d9c5d68-4d2f-4db0-a48a-48b5adf0988b",
"title": " Validate TaskFlow input ",
"description": "Schema-first validation"
}

The title received by the service is trimmed because the Zod schema produces the parsed output.

Invalid: blank title
{
"projectId": "3d9c5d68-4d2f-4db0-a48a-48b5adf0988b",
"title": "     "
}

Figure 2 - Blank-title failure
raw body

↓

trim title

↓

empty string

↓

min(1) fails

↓

400 response

The Project lookup never runs because shape validation fails earlier.

Invalid: malformed projectId
{
"projectId": "project-123",
"title": "Should not reach the service"
}

This fails UUID syntax validation. That is different from a syntactically valid UUID that simply does not identify
an existing Project; the latter reaches TasksService and becomes a Project-not-found business result.

Invalid: unknown property
{
"projectId": "3d9c5d68-4d2f-4db0-a48a-48b5adf0988b",
"title": "Should fail",
"admin": true
}

Why this matters

Strict request schemas make accidental contract expansion visible. They also stop a client from believing arbitrary
extra fields influence server behavior.

PowerShell testing
A browser UI is not required to prove the boundary. Keep testing the backend independently.

$body = @{
projectId = "<PROJECT-ID>"
title = "Validated from PowerShell"
} | ConvertTo-Json

Invoke-RestMethod `
-Method Post `
-Uri "http://localhost:4000/tasks" `
-ContentType "application/json" `
-Body $body

Update Task Validation
PATCH semantics, optional fields, nullable values, enums, and empty-update
rejection

Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
PATCH body

↓

updateTaskSchema

↓

service

↓

Prisma update

Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic.

PATCH /tasks/:id - partial updates have different
semantics
Create and update inputs are related but not identical. POST requires the fields needed to create a new Task.
PATCH represents a partial change to an existing Task.

Field                                 POST create                        PATCH update

projectId                             required                           not editable in this phase

title                                 required                           optional

description                           optional                           optional / nullable

status                                defaulted by DB/domain             optional enum update

priority                              defaulted by DB/domain             optional enum update

Valid partial update
{
"status": "IN_PROGRESS",
"priority": "HIGH"
}

Invalid enum
{
"status": "ALMOST_DONE"
}

The API vocabulary is the domain enum. A typo or invented state should be rejected before Prisma receives it.

Empty PATCH body
{}

Every property is optional, but the object itself must contain at least one supported field. The refinement rule
rejects a no-op PATCH.

Clearing a nullable field
{
"description": null
}

Because null is explicitly allowed, this request means “clear the description.” Omitting description means “leave
the current description unchanged.”

Why not derive update with .partial() blindly?
Zod can derive a partial object, and that is useful. But update contracts often diverge from create contracts:
immutable fields may disappear, different fields may become editable, and empty updates may need rejection.
Explicit update schemas can be easier to reason about in business APIs.

Design principle

Prefer a schema that expresses the real HTTP contract over maximum schema cleverness. Reuse small field
schemas such as taskTitleSchema when it improves consistency without hiding meaning.

Path, Query & Unknown-Field
Validation
UUID parameters, query coercion mental model, strict objects, and layered boundary
defense

Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
path/query/body input

↓

schema policy

↓

validated values

Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic.

Validate every external entry point deliberately
Request bodies are only one input source. Path parameters, query strings, headers, and eventually uploaded
files all cross trust boundaries. The validation technique depends on the input and phase.

UUID path parameters
export const taskIdSchema = z.uuid();

@Param("id", { schema: taskIdSchema }) id: string

The same schema is reused by GET, PATCH, and DELETE, making the route contract consistent.

Query parameters arrive as strings
We intentionally postpone the full Task filtering API until Phase 15, but the mental model starts here. A URL
such as ?page=2 still enters as text. If the handler wants a number, the schema must coerce or parse it
intentionally.

const pageSchema = z.coerce.number().int().positive();

// "2" -> 2
// "banana" -> validation failure

Transformation needs intention

Coercion is convenient, but do not coerce every malformed input into something valid. Decide which representations
your API deliberately accepts.

Unknown fields: reject, strip, or preserve?
Policy                       Behavior                            When it can make sense

Reject                       400 on unexpected property          Strict APIs, catch client mistakes early

Strip                        Remove unknown properties           Compatibility-oriented form payloads

Preserve                     Keep extras                         Extensible metadata contracts

TaskFlow Phase 12 chooses reject for write DTOs using z.strictObject. This is a contract choice, not a
universal law.

Prototype pollution and framework boundaries
NestJS itself includes protections around request transformation and dangerous prototype keys. Validation still
matters because security hardening and semantic correctness are different concerns: “this object cannot
poison a prototype” does not mean “this is a valid Task request.”

Figure 1 - Layered boundary defense
HTTP framework parsing

↓

framework safety checks

↓

schema validation

↓

business authorization/rules later

↓

database constraints

Security and correctness come from layered controls, not one magical validator.

Validation Errors, Testing & Debugging
Diagnose failures by layer and prove malformed input never reaches persistence

Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
invalid request

↓

validation failure

↓

400 response

Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic.

What a validation failure should mean
At this phase, invalid request shape should produce a client error before business logic executes. We keep
NestJS's framework-provided validation response rather than designing a custom enterprise error envelope
prematurely; Phase 13 will standardize application errors.

Figure 1 - Error ownership
Malformed input

↓

StandardSchemaValidationPipe

↓

400 Bad Request

↓

client fixes request

Shape errors are client contract failures, not database failures.

Do not expose raw database errors for input mistakes
If a malformed enum reaches Prisma and Prisma rejects it, the architecture has already allowed invalid external
data too far into the system. The client should learn about contract errors at the boundary, not from persistence
internals.

Diagnostic sequence
Symptom                                                    First question

Invalid body still reaches service                         Is the global StandardSchemaValidationPipe registered?

Schema seems ignored                                       Did @Body/@Param attach schema metadata?

Valid request fails                                        Which exact Zod issue failed?

Unknown field is accepted                                  Did you use a strict object schema?

PATCH {} succeeds                                          Did the update schema refine against empty objects?

UUID validation fails for real IDs                         Does the persisted ID format match the schema?

Testing malformed requests systematically
• missing required field

• wrong primitive type

• blank string after trimming

• string above maximum length

• invalid UUID

• invalid enum member

• unknown property

• empty PATCH object

• valid null for a nullable field

• fully valid request still persists

Representative request matrix
Request                                         Expected layer                      Expected outcome

POST title=false                                schema                              400

POST projectId=bad-uuid                         schema                              400

POST valid UUID but Project missing             service                             404

GET /tasks/not-a-uuid                           schema                              400

GET /tasks/                                     service                             404

PATCH {}                                        schema                              400

PATCH status=ALMOST_DONE                        schema                              400

PATCH status=DONE                               service/Prisma                      success if Task exists

400 and 404 tell different stories

400 says the request does not satisfy the endpoint contract. 404 says the request was structurally valid, but the
referenced application resource was not found.

Shared Schemas & Boundary Design
When to share validation, why transport schemas are not Prisma models, and
avoiding premature packages

Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
API transport contract

↓

application/domain rules

↓

persistence model

Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic.

Should Zod schemas be shared with Next.js now?
Zod can run in both Node.js and browsers, so it is tempting to immediately move every schema into
packages/validators. That may eventually be useful, but Phase 12 does not create a shared package merely
because sharing is possible.

Question                                                         If yes...

Does the frontend need exactly the same request contract?        A shared schema may reduce drift.

Does moving the schema create package/build complexity now?      Keep it API-local until the benefit is concrete.

Does the backend schema import server-only generated Prisma      Avoid shipping server coupling into a browser package.
code?

Would a shared transport schema be stable across clients?        Shared validation may become valuable.

Our current task schemas import generated Prisma enums. That is convenient inside the API but is also a
signal that blindly exporting the file to a browser package could couple frontend code to backend persistence
generation.

A future shared-contract direction
Figure 1 - Possible later evolution
packages/validators: transport-only schemas

↓

apps/web imports browser-safe request schema

↓

apps/api imports same transport schema

↓

NestJS service maps validated transport data to domain/persistence

Share a contract because multiple consumers genuinely need it, not because the monorepo has a packages folder.

Validation schema is not your database model
A transport schema describes what an API caller may send. Prisma schema describes durable relational
structure. They overlap, but they should not be treated as identical artifacts.

Transport/API concern                                        Database concern

title max length policy                                      column type / persisted value

unknown request keys                                         not applicable to row schema

PATCH omits unchanged field                                  UPDATE operation semantics

projectId must be UUID text                                  foreign key relation must reference existing Project

Architecture rule

Do not make the frontend speak Prisma. Do not make Prisma schema the HTTP API. Let each boundary have the
representation that matches its responsibility.

Avoid validation duplication inside service methods
Once a service is only callable through validated controllers, it can often assume transport shape correctness.
But service methods may later be reused by jobs, CLI tools, tests, or internal workflows. At that point, decide
whether those callers need their own validated boundary or a stronger domain-level invariant. Do not simply
sprinkle schema.parse() everywhere.

Hands-on lab
Complete the lab against the running Phase 11 TaskFlow API. The goal is not only to make valid requests
succeed; you must prove invalid data is rejected at the intended layer.

Lab A - Install and wire validation
• From apps/api install zod@4.6.5.

• Register StandardSchemaValidationPipe globally in main.ts.

• Create tasks.schemas.ts.

• Remove the temporary tasks.types.ts once controller/service imports have been migrated.

• Build the API before running it.

Lab B - Create schema tests
Payload                                                                 Expected

valid projectId + title                                                 201

missing title                                                           400

title with only spaces                                                  400

title > 200 chars                                                       400

projectId not UUID                                                      400

unknown admin field                                                     400

valid UUID for missing Project                                          404

Lab C - Update schema tests
Payload                                                                 Expected

{"status":"DONE"}                                                       success for existing Task

{"status":"ALMOST_DONE"}                                                400

{"description":null}                                                    success; clear description

{}                                                                      400

{"projectId":"..."}                                                     400 unknown field

Lab D - Path parameter tests
• GET /tasks/not-a-uuid should return 400 without querying the service for a Task.

• GET /tasks/ should pass validation and then return 404 from application logic.

• PATCH and DELETE should apply the same UUID contract.

Exercise levels

Level                     Challenge

1 - Follow                Reproduce the reference schemas exactly and pass the matrix.

2 - Modify                Lower title max length temporarily and observe the boundary behavior, then restore it.

3 - Implement             Add a validated dueAt transport field with an intentional accepted format; map it safely into the service.

4 - Engineer              Design whether TaskFlow should reject or strip unknown fields in public API v1, and defend the decision
with compatibility and debugging trade-offs.

Architecture oral exam
• Why can a TypeScript interface not validate JSON arriving over HTTP?

• What does StandardSchemaValidationPipe do, and what does the route decorator schema option do?

• Why does a valid UUID for a missing Project become 404 rather than 400?

• What is the semantic difference between omitted description and description: null in PATCH?

• Why should TaskFlow not automatically move all Zod schemas into packages/validators today?

• Which layer should verify that an assignee belongs to the same Workspace as the Task?

Phase exit checklist
• zod is installed and locked at 4.6.5.

• global StandardSchemaValidationPipe is active.

• create/update/path schemas are attached to controller inputs.

• unknown body fields are rejected.

• valid data still persists through Prisma.

• invalid shape does not reach TasksService.

• API build passes.

• you can explain validation vs business rule vs database constraint without looking at the book.

Untrusted HTTP input

↓

Zod / Standard Schema validation

↓

TasksController

↓

TasksService

↓

PrismaService

↓

Supabase PostgreSQL

Phase 13 will make errors professional across the whole API: consistent error structure, exception boundaries,
Prisma conflict translation, request correlation, and what should or should not be exposed to clients.

Guided Build Lab — Phase 12: DTOs, Zod & Input Validation

Purpose

Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything.

Architecture trace
untrusted JSON/query -> schema parse -> typed validated value -> business rules -> persistence

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Debugging Workshop — Phase 12: DTOs, Zod & Input Validation

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
untrusted JSON/query -> schema parse -> typed validated value -> business rules -> persistence

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Assuming TypeScript validates runtime JSON
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Duplicating client and server validation rules without a sharing strategy
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Putting database existence checks into pure syntax schemas
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — Accepting arbitrary unknown keys into persistence calls
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — DTOs, Zod & Input Validation

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 12 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Validate untrusted input with Zod and DTO/boundary patterns while keeping transport validation distinct from business rules.

Required artifact
Reusable create/update/query schemas integrated into NestJS request handling with useful validation errors.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can distinguish type checking from runtime validation.
• Can build create/update/query schemas.
• Can map Zod failures to HTTP responses.
• Can identify domain rules that belong after validation.

Independent build sequence
1. List the exact fields accepted by create-task and reject unknown/invalid shapes deliberately.
2. Create a Zod schema and derive the TypeScript type instead of maintaining two divergent contracts.
3. Integrate validation at the NestJS boundary before the service receives data.
4. Create a partial update schema carefully and reason about omitted vs nullable fields.
5. Validate query parameters such as page size/sort values instead of trusting strings.
6. Send malformed requests and verify the error contract is actionable but does not expose internals.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 12: DTOs, Zod & Input Validation. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
Reusable create/update/query schemas integrated into NestJS request handling with useful validation errors.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.
